about: The first five theories (CP4). Each has the plain-language text the Planner gets, one paraphrase, and the gold answer the Planner's spec is reviewed against (Assumption 1: right variables, sign, unit of analysis). Texts avoid column names on purpose (CP4 audit W5). chr_* columns come from County Health Rankings (Vien, V2); until they are in the panel, those theories cannot run.

theories.text: Watchdog-style financial ratings are unfair to nonprofits that work in hard-pressed places: organizations in the most economically distressed quarter of counties get lower scores on the usual 0-10 financial score.
theories.paraphrase: If you score nonprofits the way charity watchdogs do, the ones based in the worst-off local economies come out worse.
theories.why: The CP3 theory; the hand-written spec specs/ratings_fairness.json is its gold standard.

theories.text: Nonprofits in places where people are in worse health are stretched thinner: they end the year with smaller surpluses relative to their income.
theories.paraphrase: Poor community health eats into nonprofits' bottom line.
theories.why: Demand pressure: more need for services on the same revenue base (resource dependency).

theories.text: In better-educated communities it costs nonprofits less to bring in each donated dollar.
theories.paraphrase: Where more residents have been to college, fundraising pays off more cheaply.
theories.why: A wealthier, more giving local donor base.

theories.text: Nonprofits in more violent places spend a bigger slice of their budget on running the organization itself rather than on programs or fundraising.
theories.paraphrase: High local crime pushes up nonprofits' overhead.
theories.why: Security, insurance and staff turnover costs.

theories.text: Where joblessness is high, nonprofits owe more relative to what they own.
theories.paraphrase: Local job losses leave nonprofits carrying heavier debt loads.
theories.why: Financial vulnerability under local economic stress (Tuckman and Chang).
